title: Hundred Dollar Baby

jokes.text: Mac declares Rocky IV is 'probably the greatest movie of all time' — Dee suggests Million Dollar Baby, which won an Oscar; Mac and Charlie dismiss it because 'girls can't fight'
jokes.setup: The gang is debating greatest movies of all time with apparent seriousness
jokes.punchline: Their cinematic analysis boils down to Rocky IV being superior because Stallone 'bashes a Russian's face to all smithereens' — an Oscar win is dismissed as irrelevant
jokes.explanation: Strong cold open that immediately establishes the gang's idiotic worldview. The juxtaposition of an Oscar vs. 'bashing a Russian's face to smithereens' as competing metrics of quality is perfectly character-specific — only these guys would have this debate this earnestly.

jokes.text: 'GIRLS CAN'T PULL TRUCKS THROUGH SNOW.' / 'CAN YOU PULL TRUCKS THROUGH SNOW?' / 'I ABSOLUTELY COULD.'
jokes.setup: Mac says girls can't fight because they don't have muscles; Dee pushes back calling it sexist
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to the specific metric of pulling trucks through snow; Dee, offended by the sexism, immediately claims she absolutely could do it — ironically accepting the absurd premise
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-structured comedic exchange. The joke is that Dee, in defending herself against sexism, earnestly claims she can do an objectively absurd thing. The truck-through-snow specificity elevates it above generic gender-argument comedy. Quick and punchy — excellent economy.

jokes.text: Mac's argument that Million Dollar Baby is unrealistic because 'Girls can't fight. They don't have muscles. It's true.'
jokes.setup: Mac is criticizing Million Dollar Baby's premise
jokes.punchline: 'It's true' delivered as a sincere factual clarification, not a sexist remark — in Mac's mind he is being helpful
jokes.explanation: The 'It's true' tag is what elevates this — Mac genuinely believes he's correcting a misconception, not being sexist. Perfect character-driven obliviousness.

jokes.text: Charlie interrupts the truck-pulling argument to ask 'TIME OUT. IS THE TRUCK PARKED IN NEUTRAL?' followed immediately by 'EMPTY YOUR POCKETS.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are arguing about whether Dee could pull a truck through snow; Charlie seems to be engaging with the debate by asking about the truck's gear
jokes.punchline: The 'empty your pockets' line reveals they are being mugged mid-argument — Charlie's neutral question was asked of the mugger, not in the debate
jokes.explanation: Exceptional misdirection. The transcript makes the audience (and reader) believe Charlie is asking about the truck hypothetical; the 'empty your pockets' recontextualizes everything. Structurally near-perfect — the reveal lands hard, the economy is ruthless. A rewatch bonus because you re-evaluate the neutral question.

jokes.text: Dee says 'NICE FRIENDS' sarcastically after being abandoned with the mugger
jokes.setup: Mac, Charlie, and Dennis have ditched Dee with an armed mugger
jokes.punchline: Dee's only response to being left with a knife-wielding mugger is a dry, understated 'nice friends'
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny beat — the gang's sociopathy delivered with Dee's resigned sarcasm. Economy is perfect (two words), but it's a fairly standard reaction beat. Works in context.

jokes.text: The gang negotiates the truck-pulling hypothetical post-mugging: 'MAYBE... ONE TO TWO INCHES OF SNOW?' / 'ONE TO TWO INCHES... AND A FORD F-150. RIGHT. IN PARK, BUT NO EMERGENCY BRAKE. MAYBE I COULD PULL IT FOUR FEET. I'D GIVE HIM FOUR FEET. I'D GIVE HIM FIVE.'
jokes.setup: The guys have just been mugged; instead of processing the traumatic event, they resume the truck-pulling argument as if nothing happened
jokes.punchline: They are solemnly negotiating the exact parameters — snow depth, truck model, emergency brake status — of a hypothetical truck pull, arriving at a generous concession of 'five feet'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The gang's sociopathic indifference to the mugging — immediately resuming a pointless debate — is pitch-perfect Sunny. The specificity of the negotiation (F-150, no emergency brake, emergency brake distinction, four vs. five feet) escalates the absurdity beautifully. Character-specific: only these guys would do this. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: 'WHAT KIND OF QUEER SHIT IS THAT?' — Mac's response to 'Boxercise'
jokes.setup: Dee mentions she's been taking 'Boxercise' classes at the gym for self-defense
jokes.punchline: Mac's contemptuous dismissal — the word 'queer' landing as simultaneously homophobic and genuinely confused
jokes.explanation: Functional character moment for Mac — his casual homophobia/contempt is a running trait. The irony that Mac is deeply closeted (a later-series revelation) adds retroactive value, but in isolation it's a competent rather than exceptional joke.

jokes.text: 'YOU WANNA LEARN SELF-DEFENSE, YOU COME TO DADDY.' — Frank's entrance
jokes.setup: Dee is explaining she's taking Boxercise for self-defense after being mugged
jokes.punchline: Frank barges in offering to teach her, declaring himself 'Daddy' — immediately followed by his boxer backstory
jokes.explanation: Frank inserting himself into every situation as an authority is core character comedy. 'Come to Daddy' from this repulsive man is funny in its delusional confidence. Sets up the Frankie Fast Hands backstory well.

jokes.text: 'ALL DURING THE '60s, BEFORE I MET MY WHORE WIFE, I WAS A BOXER. THEY CALLED ME FRANKIE FAST HANDS.'
jokes.setup: Frank is offering his boxing credentials to train Dee
jokes.punchline: The casual, matter-of-fact insertion of 'before I met my whore wife' as a biographical data point — not an insult, just Frank's neutral description of his timeline
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the delivery — 'my whore wife' is not emphasized, it's parenthetical. Frank treats it as unremarkable biographical context, which is what makes it so funny. High character integration: this is quintessentially Frank Reynolds.

jokes.text: 'FRANKIE FAST HANDS, EVERYBODY. YEAH, KEEP LIVIN' IN THE PAST, DAD.'
jokes.setup: Frank announces his boxing nickname with apparent pride
jokes.punchline: Dennis mockingly introduces him like a failed entertainer ('Frankie Fast Hands, everybody') then dismisses him
jokes.explanation: Dennis's contempt for Frank delivered with the 'everybody' flourish is a nice touch — it mimics the MC announcing a washed-up act. Competent character comedy.

jokes.text: Mac asks if Dee's training is because of Million Dollar Baby; Dee reveals she was left with a mugger with a knife — 'YOU DITCHED YOUR SISTER?' / 'ABSOLUTELY.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks if Dee's interest in boxing is movie-inspired
jokes.punchline: Dee reveals the actually serious reason (mugging at knifepoint); Dennis's response to 'you ditched your sister?' is a flat, unapologetic 'Absolutely' with zero remorse
jokes.explanation: The 'Absolutely' is the joke — delivered without hesitation, guilt, or self-awareness. Dennis's sociopathy in one word. Character integration is excellent; this confirms the gang's moral baseline for new viewers.

jokes.text: 'TECHNIQUE DON'T MEAN SHIT OUT ON THE STREETS.' / 'AIN'T NO RULES OUT ON THE STREETS.' / 'YOU GUYS GOT NO RULES ON THE STREETS, YOU.' — Frank, Mac, Charlie competing to sound street-tough
jokes.setup: Frank claims his boxing technique would have helped against the mugger
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie co-opt Frank's tough-guy speech about 'the streets' until all three are competitively riffing on the same phrase, each one less convincingly street-tough than the last
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation — the joke compounds as each character piles on with diminishing credibility. 'You guys got no rules on the streets, you' is the comedic peak, slightly awkward in a way that's perfectly Charlie. Dee's takedown ('you three jackasses, like you've been there') lands the button well.

jokes.text: Dee calls them 'three jackasses' who talk about the streets like they've been there, then Frank sincerely adds: 'I MEAN, ANY UNDERGROUND STREET FIGHT IN PHILADELPHIA, YOU'D FIND TONS OF TECHNIQUE.'
jokes.setup: Dee shuts down the street-tough posturing with a reasonable, exasperated reality check
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately undermines the correction by earnestly defending underground street fights as a venue where technique is valued — missing her point entirely
jokes.explanation: Frank's sincere non-sequitur is funny precisely because he's not being combative — he genuinely thinks underground street fighting is a legitimate counterexample. Good character work.

jokes.text: Mac's immediate pivot: 'I mean, any underground street fight in Philadelphia, you'd find tons of technique.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just called them out for pretending to have street cred
jokes.punchline: Mac doesn't rebut the accusation — he just pivots to a new, equally unfounded specific claim about underground street fights
jokes.explanation: Mac's conversational non-sequitur pivot — ignoring the accusation and immediately launching a new assertion — is classic Mac rhetorical technique.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover an underground fight club: 'THERE'S BLOOD EVERYWHERE. IT'S BEAUTIFUL.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis follow up on Frank's underground street-fighting tip
jokes.punchline: Their rapturous aesthetic appreciation for the violence — 'it's beautiful' — treats the bloody spectacle as fine art
jokes.explanation: Dennis's psychopathic aestheticization of violence ('it's beautiful') is consistent with his character's emerging darkness. Functional but not exceptional — the show will push this further in later seasons.

jokes.text: 'YOU KNOW WHO CAN TAKE A REALLY GOOD BEATING? CHARLIE. CHARLIE.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis observe that the fight club rewards the ability to absorb punishment rather than technique
jokes.punchline: Their immediate leap to Charlie as the ideal 'guy who takes beatings' — delivered with enthusiastic agreement — implies Charlie's status as the gang's perpetual punching bag
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the repetition of 'Charlie. Charlie.' like it's the most obvious answer in the world. The joke reveals the entire power dynamic of the gang without commentary. Charlie as human punching bag is a cornerstone of the show's mythology.

jokes.text: Frank smells the gym: 'THAT'S THE SMELL OF HARD WORK. AND FEET.' / 'THAT'S THE SMELL OF BIG DREAMS. THE SMELL OF GLORY.' / 'IT SMELLS LIKE FEET. AND FEET.'
jokes.setup: Frank delivers a nostalgic, inspirational speech about the smell of the gym — invoking hard work, big dreams, glory
jokes.punchline: He undermines himself mid-speech by inserting 'and feet,' then Dee strips away all pretense: 'it smells like feet. And feet.'
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: Frank tries to do the inspirational sports-movie moment but can't stop himself from noting the foot smell, twice. Then Dee reduces the entire speech to 'feet. And feet.' The repetition of 'and feet' is the key — it's the rhythm that makes it work. Quotable.

jokes.text: Frank tells Bobby Thunderson 'You... really let yourself go' — then immediately pivots to asking if Bobby is trying to get back into fighting form
jokes.setup: Frank reunites with old boxing buddy Bobby Thunderson after years apart
jokes.punchline: Frank — himself a grotesque, out-of-shape older man — tells Bobby he's 'really let himself go,' with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Classic pot-calling-kettle joke elevated by Frank's total lack of self-awareness. The visual gag (Frank, clearly not in shape himself, lecturing Bobby) would amplify this in the actual episode. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Bobby says his daughter is 'pretty too, huh? Like her old man?' — Bobby is implied to be grotesque
jokes.setup: Bobby points out his daughter training across the gym, noting she's pretty
jokes.punchline: Bobby, who Frank just noted has 'really let himself go,' invites comparison between his daughter's attractiveness and his own — 'like her old man, huh?'
jokes.explanation: Straightforward visual/character comedy — works better on screen where Bobby's appearance is visible. In transcript form, it's readable but loses impact without the visual confirmation.

jokes.text: Bobby makes an annoying sound; Frank says 'OH, MY GOD, THAT'S AN ANNOYING SOUND HE MAKES.' / Dee: 'ASS... HOLE.' / Frank: 'YEAH, ASSHOLE.'
jokes.setup: Bobby makes some kind of obnoxious vocalization as he walks away
jokes.punchline: Frank and Dee's synchronized contempt — Frank noting it clinically, Dee delivering 'ass... hole' with a pause as if calculating whether to say it, then Frank echoing in agreement
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the shared contempt and the broken delivery of 'ass... hole' — the pause makes it funnier. A small moment, competently executed.

jokes.text: Frank describes squats: 'YOU'RE GONNA TAKE ALL THE WEIGHT ON YOUR NECK. THEN YOU'RE GONNA JAM YOUR LEGS DOWN AND HYPEREXTEND YOUR ANKLES... AND SHOOT BACK UP AND LOCK YOUR KNEES IN PLACE.'
jokes.setup: Frank is training Dee in weight lifting, claiming expertise from his boxing days
jokes.punchline: His squat technique is a list of injuries waiting to happen — every single instruction is specifically dangerous: neck load, hyperextended ankles, locked knees
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic construction — each instruction escalates the wrongness. Anyone with gym knowledge will laugh harder at each beat. Frank's confident delivery of a list of ways to destroy your spine is perfect character comedy: dangerous incompetence delivered as wisdom. Dee's response ('not one of those things sounds right') is the ideal straight-man button.

jokes.text: 'NOT ONE OF THOSE THINGS SOUNDS RIGHT TO ME AT ALL.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just described a squat technique that would cause multiple injuries
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat, comprehensive rejection — the understatement of 'not one of those things' covering what is objectively a list of medical disasters
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke. The economy is exceptional — 'not one of those things' captures everything without elaboration. Dee as reluctant straight man works well here.

jokes.text: 'AT LEAST I GOT THE ONE. RIGHT?'
jokes.setup: Dee has struggled enormously to do a single squat under Frank's catastrophic technique; she barely manages one before collapsing
jokes.punchline: Dee's pathetically optimistic framing of one failed squat rep as an achievement
jokes.explanation: The 'right?' seeking validation makes it funnier — she's genuinely asking for affirmation after a humiliation. The cringe of watching Dee completely fail while trying to prove herself is core to the episode's engine.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis pitch training Charlie by saying he's 'practically invincible' — the plan to 'smash things all over your body' as fight training
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis identify Charlie as the guy to put in underground fights because he 'can take a beating'
jokes.punchline: Their training methodology is to literally smash objects on Charlie — a trash can, potentially a chair — as 'tolerance building'
jokes.explanation: The gang's training plan being 'hit Charlie with objects' is hilariously coherent within their internal logic while being completely insane. The escalation to 'Dennis wanted to use a chair' and Charlie enthusiastically requesting the chair shows all three characters in perfect form.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis tell Charlie Rocky never wears a shirt when he trains, insisting he remove his for training; Charlie resists saying 'it feels a little gay'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis want Charlie to take his shirt off for training; they justify it via Rocky
jokes.punchline: Charlie's resistance — 'it feels a little gay' — while Mac and Dennis both insist 'it's not gay' creates an increasingly homoerotic dynamic that all parties are determinedly blind to
jokes.explanation: The running shirt joke is well-mined throughout the episode. The irony that Mac (who is gay) is insisting 'it's not gay' while trying to get Charlie shirtless is thick. Charlie asking why he can't 'passionately rip it off in the moment' is the funniest beat here — his weirdly cinematic self-image.

jokes.text: 'WHY CAN'T I JUST GET, LIKE, ALL EXCITED AND PASSIONATELY RIP IT OFF IN THE MOMENT?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis want Charlie to simply take his shirt off; Charlie refuses
jokes.punchline: Charlie's alternative vision of himself dramatically and passionately ripping his shirt off in a moment of athletic inspiration — he has an entire romantic narrative about this
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest lines. Charlie has constructed an entire inner life around the moment of shirt removal — it must be earned through passion and excitement, not just requested. The gap between Charlie's cinematic self-image and his actual status as the gang's punching bag is the heart of his character. Highly quotable, entirely specific to Charlie.

jokes.text: Charlie punches the board and fails — 'WHAT'S THAT MADE OUT OF?' / 'IT'S A BOARD, SO IT'S, YOU KNOW, MADE OUT OF WOOD.' / 'IT'S PARTICLE BOARD.' / 'NO, IT'S ACTUALLY SOFTER THAN WOOD.' / 'PETRIFIED WOOD.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have Charlie punch a board as training; he fails to break it and injures himself
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis scramble to rationalize why Charlie couldn't break it — cycling through 'particle board' (harder than wood), then correcting to 'actually softer than wood,' then Mac offering 'petrified wood' as a final escalation
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny verbal escalation. The rationalizations contradict each other ('harder than wood' / 'actually softer than wood') and culminate in the absurd non-solution of 'petrified wood' — which would actually be harder. Mac and Dennis's need to protect their plan from evidence of its failure is well-characterized.

jokes.text: 'I WASN'T DRUNK ENOUGH. YOU SHOULD BE DRUNK FOR THIS.' / 'WE SHOULD ALL BE DRUNK FOR THIS. LET'S GET REALLY DRUNK.'
jokes.setup: Charlie fails to break the board and is in pain
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate diagnosis is insufficient alcohol; Mac enthusiastically extends this to all of them; they pivot training to getting drunk
jokes.explanation: The gang's solution to every problem being alcohol is a character staple; this instance is elevated because it's framed as a training methodology. 'We should all be drunk for this' escalates it perfectly. Mac's enthusiasm to join in ('let's get really drunk') is very Mac.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis let Charlie go get beer alone — silent reaction beat as they watch him leave, implying they're keeping him away while they discuss something
jokes.setup: Charlie goes to get beers; Mac says 'Let him go'
jokes.punchline: The conspiratorial pause — Mac and Dennis clearly have a separate agenda they don't want Charlie present for
jokes.explanation: A structural beat that sets up the ongoing manipulation of Charlie. Functional rather than funny on its own, but serves the episode's comedic architecture.

jokes.text: Bobby tells Frank about their 1961 fight: 'THEY BILLED IT AS BEAUTY VERSUS THE BEAST.' — implying Frank was the beast
jokes.setup: Bobby starts reminiscing about their old fight, billing it as 'Beauty versus the Beast'
jokes.punchline: The implication is obvious — Frank was the Beast — which Bobby confirms by saying Frank 'went down like a...' before getting interrupted
jokes.explanation: The 'Beauty versus the Beast' label with Frank as the beast is a standard insult-comedy beat. The interrupted 'he went down like a...' teases the callback. Competent, not exceptional.

jokes.text: 'EXCUSES ARE LIKE ASSHOLES. EVERYBODY'S GOT ONE, AND THEY ALL STINK.'
jokes.setup: Frank accuses Bobby of hitting him after the bell — a cheap shot
jokes.punchline: Bobby deploys the 'excuses are like assholes' cliché in the middle of an actual fight promotion scene
jokes.explanation: A lazy, well-worn cliché delivered straight. It works as Bobby characterization (he's a blowhard who uses stock phrases) but isn't clever writing. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: 'I LET MY DAUGHTER DO MY FIGHTING FOR ME.' / 'AND MAYBE IN A COUPLE YEARS, WHEN THIS LITTLE GRAHAM CRACKER MIGHT HAVE THE STUFF TO COMPETE...'
jokes.setup: Bobby says he doesn't fight anymore in his old age
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he's training his daughter to fight for him — and dismisses Dee as a 'little Graham Cracker' who might not be ready in a couple years
jokes.explanation: 'Graham cracker' as a dismissive nickname for Dee is funny — contemptuous but weirdly specific and mild. Bobby using his daughter as a proxy fighter is the right amount of absurd. Solid character-building for the antagonist.

jokes.text: Dee confronts Bobby, who calls her 'LITTLE BUTTERCUP' and tells her not to get her 'PANTIES IN AN UPROAR'
jokes.setup: Dee stands up to Bobby on Frank's behalf, calling him out
jokes.punchline: Bobby's condescending pet names — 'little buttercup,' 'panties in an uproar' — are patronizing enough to be infuriating AND funny
jokes.explanation: Bobby's condescension escalates the cringe. 'Little buttercup' is a funny choice — both diminutive and weirdly floral for a gym context. Functional antagonist comedy.

jokes.text: A mysterious woman approaches Dee in the gym shadows: 'IF ONLY THERE WAS A WAY THAT YOU COULD BE... PHYSICALLY TOUGH ENOUGH TO INTIMIDATE MEN.' / 'STEP INTO THE SHADOWS AND, UH, WE'LL TALK.'
jokes.setup: Dee is venting about men pushing her around after Bobby's condescension
jokes.punchline: A stranger appears with a suspiciously on-the-nose offer to solve Dee's exact problem, capping it with 'step into the shadows' — a parodically obvious drug dealer introduction
jokes.explanation: The 'step into the shadows' line is the punchline — it's a knowing parody of every after-school special drug-dealing scene. The dealer's pitch perfectly mirrors Dee's stated problem, which makes it funnier. The deadpan absurdity of this happening in a gym is well-played.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis wake up Charlie by knocking and then hitting him with the trash can when he opens the door: 'SURPRISE, BITCH.' / 'YOU'RE HITTIN' ME WITH THAT?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis announce their training plan to build Charlie's tolerance to punishment
jokes.punchline: They immediately demonstrate the plan by hitting Charlie with a trash can the second he opens the door
jokes.explanation: 'Surprise, bitch' as a greeting while hitting someone with a trash can is perfectly economical. The plan-becomes-immediate-action structure is well-executed. Charlie's confused 'you're hitting me with that?' shows he's not even surprised they're hitting him, just puzzled about the specific implement.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis explain Charlie's training: 'IT'S NOT GONNA BE ABOUT INFLICTING PUNISHMENT, IT'S GONNA BE ABOUT HAVING PUNISHMENT INFLICTED UPON YOU. WE NEED TO SMASH THINGS ALL OVER YOUR BODY.'
jokes.setup: Charlie punching boards didn't work; Mac and Dennis present their new strategy
jokes.punchline: Their reframing of 'getting beaten up' as a legitimate training methodology, delivered with complete sincerity and a kind of inspiring sports-movie cadence
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'inflicting' to 'having punishment inflicted upon you' is delivered like a genuine insight — Mac and Dennis have convinced themselves this is sound sports science. The sincerity elevates what could be a simple abuse joke.

jokes.text: 'CHARLIE, GO PUT ON THOSE LITTLE SHORT-SHORTS. LET'S TAKE THINGS TO THE NEXT LEVEL.' / 'BUT FIRST THINGS FIRST. LET'S GET GOOD AND DRUNK.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are escalating Charlie's training regimen
jokes.punchline: The 'next level' turns out to be: short-shorts + drunk. These are their training priorities.
jokes.explanation: The return of alcohol as the foundational training methodology, now with the addition of short-shorts as the athletic wardrobe requirement. The 'next level' framing against the actual content is the joke. Mac's homoerotic short-shorts request is consistent with his character.

jokes.text: Mac: 'But first things first — let's get good and drunk!' All three: 'LET'S GET DRUNK!'
jokes.setup: Mac is building to some training milestone
jokes.punchline: Getting drunk is again presented as the first priority of athletic training, now with unanimous celebration
jokes.explanation: The callback to drunk training, now with everyone on board, is a weaker version of the first beat. Still works as a running gag payoff.

jokes.text: The steroid dealer explains the pills: 'THESE AREN'T STEROIDS... THESE ARE PERFORMANCE-ENHANCING SUPPLEMENTS.' / 'YOU'LL FEEL IT ALMOST IMMEDIATELY... YOU MAY EXPERIENCE SOME MOOD SWINGS, SOME IRRATIONAL THINKING...'
jokes.setup: Dee is being sold steroids
jokes.punchline: The dealer's euphemism 'performance-enhancing supplements' alongside a side-effect list that is precisely steroids (mood swings, irrational thinking)
jokes.explanation: Standard 'denial that describes the thing' joke. The 'performance-enhancing supplements' euphemism is well-worn but lands because it's delivered so earnestly. Competent setup for Dee's later roid-rage behavior.

jokes.text: 'WHICH ARE WHAT?' / 'YOU EVER PUNCHED A GUY SO HARD IN THE EYE HE SWALLOWED IT?'
jokes.setup: Dee asks about the long-term effects of the 'supplements'
jokes.punchline: The dealer's impossibly violent hypothetical — punching a guy's eye into his throat — delivered as if it's a known, achievable outcome
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and among the best single lines in the series. The question 'you ever punched a guy so hard in the eye he swallowed it?' is anatomically impossible, delivered with total calm, as a sales pitch. The economy is surgical — no word wasted, the absurdist image is perfectly specific. It becomes the benchmark for the steroid payoff. Highly quotable, dark, and completely original in its specificity.

jokes.text: 'I'LL GET SOME WATER.' — Dee's response after the eye-swallowing pitch
jokes.setup: The dealer has just described punching someone's eye into their throat as a selling point
jokes.punchline: Dee's immediate, matter-of-fact pivot to getting water — she has accepted the offer, a decision communicated entirely by this mundane response
jokes.explanation: Perfect punchline to the dealer's pitch. Three words communicate everything: Dee has decided to take the steroids, her decision-making process took approximately zero seconds, and 'getting some water' is the most mundane possible response to being promised the ability to punch eyes down throats. The understatement is total. Exceptional economy.

jokes.text: The shirt argument continues — Charlie refuses to take his shirt off at Mac's request; Mac says 'You're ruining the moment'; Charlie says 'What is with you and the moment?'
jokes.setup: Mac wants Charlie to remove his shirt before they punch him
jokes.punchline: Charlie has turned Mac's earlier 'the moment' language back on him — now they're both arguing about 'the moment' as if it's a real concept with agreed-upon rules
jokes.explanation: The running gag pays off here — 'What is with you and the moment?' is Charlie calling Mac on his own framing. The shirt becomes a philosophical object. Good running-gag mechanics.

jokes.text: Mac punches Charlie without warning; Charlie says 'Well, you caught me off guard. That was a big part of it.'
jokes.setup: They've agreed to have Mac punch Charlie; Mac is waiting for the shirt; Charlie says 'who do you want to punch first?'
jokes.punchline: Mac just punches him mid-sentence; Charlie's diplomatic analysis of why the punch hurt ('you caught me off guard — that was a big part of it') implies he would have been fine otherwise
jokes.explanation: Charlie's earnest, analytical post-punch debrief is very funny — 'that was a big part of it' implies a measured multi-factor assessment of why he reacted poorly to being punched in the face. Character-specific Charlie behavior. The 'same spot' follow-up adds a nice button.

jokes.text: 'CHARLIE, IF WE KEEP THIS UP, YOU'RE GONNA BE THE BEST UNDERGROUND STREET FIGHTER EVER, BRO.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have been punching Charlie repeatedly
jokes.punchline: Mac's sincere inspirational speech delivered after what is essentially a session of them punching their friend — the gap between the inspiring framing and the abuse is the joke
jokes.explanation: Functional irony — the inspirational framing around abuse. Competent but not among the episode's stronger moments.

jokes.text: Dee, now on steroids, is pushing herself dangerously hard; Frank tries to stop her — Dee explodes: 'YOU THINK I CAN'T DO THIS BY MYSELF? YOU THINK I'M ON SOMETHING?' / Frank: 'I never said you were on something.' / Dee: 'THEN DON'T. DON'T START.'
jokes.setup: Frank notes Dee has changed in the last few days and seems to be overdoing it
jokes.punchline: Dee's pre-emptive, paranoid denial ('you think I'm on something?') in response to a question that wasn't asked — confirming she is very obviously on something
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic-irony cringe comedy — the audience knows she's on steroids, Frank is figuring it out, and Dee is betraying herself with every word. 'Then don't. Don't start.' to a question he didn't ask is the perfect roid-rage paranoia.

jokes.text: 'YOU LOOK LIKE A HOLOCAUST VICTIM IN PAGEANT MAKEUP.' — Bobby to Dee
jokes.setup: Bobby observes the roid-raged Dee who has been training excessively
jokes.punchline: Bobby's insult is specifically constructed — 'holocaust victim' (skeletal) plus 'pageant makeup' (incongruously glamorous) — a vivid, mean, specific image
jokes.explanation: Genuinely dark and specific — the combination of two clashing images creates a funny-horrible portrait. It's a character-revealing insult (Bobby is cruel and specific) and a Dee-revealing one (she looks manic and over-made-up). The show's dark-subversive tone at a solid medium level.

jokes.text: 'I WILL EAT YOUR BABIES, BITCH.' — Dee's response to Bobby's insult
jokes.setup: Bobby insults Dee viciously; Dee is now fully roid-raged
jokes.punchline: The threat to eat babies is completely disproportionate — it's not a fighting threat, it's a primal, unhinged escalation that reveals the steroids have taken over Dee's brain entirely
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode and among the show's most quotable moments. The threat to 'eat your babies' as a boxing trash-talk response is perfectly absurd — it's the kind of threat that only emerges when someone has completely lost their mind. Dee saying 'bitch' after such a primal threat is a great rhythm choice. Highly quotable, completely original, Dee-specific in context.

jokes.text: 'NOBODY'S EATING BABIES.' — Frank, calmly
jokes.setup: Dee has threatened to eat Bobby's babies; Bobby says 'bring it'
jokes.punchline: Frank's calm, matter-of-fact intervention — 'nobody's eating babies' — as if this needs to be stated aloud as a de-escalation strategy
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the baby-eating threat. Frank's calm assertion functions as both literal statement (true: nobody is eating babies) and absurdist de-escalation. The delivery — matter-of-fact, as if mediating a reasonable dispute — elevates it. Three words, maximum impact. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Dee: 'What's the matter, Frankie FAT Hands?' — deliberately mispronouncing Frank's nickname in the heat of battle
jokes.setup: Bobby taunts Frank about being afraid his daughter will get knocked out
jokes.punchline: Dee misremembers/deliberately mutates Frank's boxing nickname from 'Frankie Fast Hands' to 'Frankie FAT Hands' — either through roid-rage confusion or as a deliberate insult
jokes.explanation: The nickname callback with the small, devastating change — 'Fat' instead of 'Fast' — works on multiple levels. It could be Dee's roid-brain misremembering or a deliberate insult. Either way, the specific change lands. Good callback craftsmanship.

jokes.text: 'I'M GONNA PARALYZE THIS BITCH.' — Dee, stalking toward training
jokes.setup: Dee has just had an explosive gym confrontation and committed to fighting Bobby's daughter
jokes.punchline: Instead of a typical sports-movie 'I'm gonna win' declaration, roid-raged Dee promises to cause permanent physical injury
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum dark comedy. The specificity of 'paralyze' — not 'beat,' not 'destroy,' but causing specific permanent damage — signals how completely the steroids have altered Dee's psychology. Delivered with what must be terrifying sincerity. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Full 'You're the Best Around' training montage — the gang training to the Karate Kid anthem as parody
jokes.setup: The episode has been setting up two parallel training arcs (Dee and Charlie) as parodies of sports movies
jokes.punchline: The show deploys the actual 'You're the Best Around' (the Karate Kid/Rocky-adjacent training montage song) over shots of their genuinely terrible, depraved training — trash cans, drunk punching, dangerous squats
jokes.explanation: The montage is structural comedy — using the clichéd sports-movie form against content that grotesquely violates its spirit. Using the actual licensed song from an actual training montage movie is a commitment that pays off. The rewatch bonus is high because knowing the song's context enriches every cut. Structurally the episode's most ambitious joke.

jokes.text: Dee can't find her headband; furiously rants at her dad on the phone; punches a hole in her wall: 'I JUST PUNCHED A HOLE IN MY WALL!'
jokes.setup: Post-montage, Dee is preparing for the fight — the steroids have made her completely unhinged over a headband color
jokes.punchline: The roid rage escalates from missing headband → argument with dad → accidental wall destruction, which she announces with confused surprise: 'I just punched a hole in my wall!'
jokes.explanation: The steroid payoff is landing well. Dee's surprised discovery that she just punched through a wall — 'I just punched a hole in my wall!' said as if reporting a minor anomaly — is the right level of unhinged. The headband argument as the trigger for property destruction is good escalation.

jokes.text: Dee in a headband panic: 'I'm trying to find my goddamn headband. Is that okay? Is it okay with you if I find my headband before I come down there? Is that all right with you, Dad? Jesus!'
jokes.setup: Frank calls to check on Dee before the fight
jokes.punchline: The disproportionate, escalating rage about a headband — the intensity of the response vs. the triviality of the subject
jokes.explanation: Dee's roid rage manifesting over a headband is a great escalation of her character arc. The repeated questions ('Is that okay? Is it okay with you?') simulate the looping, paranoid thinking of someone on too many stimulants.

jokes.text: Charlie is on steroids and can barely articulate his rage: 'I START THINKING, YOU KNOW, AND IT MAKES... IT MAKES ME SO ANGRY.' / 'WHAT AM I SAYING?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis check on Charlie before the fight; he seems unstable
jokes.punchline: Charlie tries to explain his steroid rage but loses the thought mid-sentence, then observes 'what am I saying?' — the steroids have destroyed his ability to maintain a coherent line of thought
jokes.explanation: Charlie's particular brand of inarticulate rage is perfectly rendered here. 'I start thinking, you know, and it makes... it makes me so angry' — what does thinking make him angry about? He doesn't know. 'What am I saying?' lands beautifully because it's the most honest possible assessment of his mental state. Character-specific to Charlie's already tenuous grip on logic.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis baby-talk Charlie into eating his eggs and promise to meet him later, then immediately bolt
jokes.setup: Charlie is on the edge of a roid-rage breakdown; Mac and Dennis need to get to the fight to sign him up
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis treat the volatile, possibly dangerous Charlie like a large toddler — 'eat some of the sandwich,' 'can you meet us later?' — and physically flee the moment he agrees
jokes.explanation: The baby-talk dynamic — soothing an enraged steroid user like you'd calm a confused child — is well-executed. Dennis and Mac's immediate exit after securing Charlie's agreement has great comedic timing (inferred from the transcript structure).

jokes.text: Fight registration: 'AND WHAT IS THIS?' / 'THESE ARE WAIVER FORMS IN CASE YOUR FIGHTER IS SERIOUSLY INJURED... OR KILLED.' / 'OH, WE DON'T CARE ABOUT THAT. SIGN AWAY.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are registering Charlie (Clown Baby) for the underground fight
jokes.punchline: The waiver covers death; Mac and Dennis waive it without hesitation or even a beat of consideration
jokes.explanation: The 'we don't care about that' response to a death waiver is a perfect expression of the gang's sociopathy toward Charlie. No hesitation, no dark joke about it — just pure practical indifference to their friend's potential death. High character integration.

jokes.text: Mac names Charlie 'CLOWN BABY' — the ensuing argument about whether it's 'baby clown' or 'clown baby'
jokes.setup: The fight organizer asks for the fighter's name
jokes.punchline: Mac has named Charlie 'Clown Baby' — the organizer's confused 'like a baby clown?' triggers a pedantic argument about the distinction between a clown that is a baby vs. a baby that is a clown
jokes.explanation: The absurdist argument about modifier order — 'clown baby' vs. 'baby clown' — is very funny because both parties are wrong to be having this argument and both have committed positions. The fight organizer's bewilderment ('what in the hell kind of name is Clown Baby?') and Mac's brilliant strategic explanation (nobody bets on 'Clown Baby') makes the name choice itself coherent within the gang's logic.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis argue: 'You mean like a baby clown?' / 'Not a baby clown. A clown ba... it's like a baby... it's like a clown that is a baby.' / 'I said Cl... Clown Baby.' / 'You said baby clown.'
jokes.setup: Mac registers the fighter as 'Clown Baby'; Dennis misheard 'Baby Clown'
jokes.punchline: The completely unresolvable semantic debate about whether a clown-baby compound prioritizes the clown or the baby — both men arguing about something that matters to nobody
jokes.explanation: The clown/baby compound word debate is very funny because it's genuinely ambiguous and also completely meaningless. Mac's inability to explain the distinction ('it's like a clown that IS a baby') while maintaining authority is excellent. The official's 'I don't even care' finally ending it is a perfect button.

jokes.text: '500 BUCKS ON CLOWN BABY.' / 'DENNIS. 500? THAT'S ALL WE GOT, DUDE.' / 'YOU SAW CHARLIE. WE TURNED THAT KID INTO AN ANIMAL.'
jokes.setup: Mac explains the Clown Baby strategy; Dennis immediately bets all their money on Charlie winning
jokes.punchline: Dennis's total confidence in their training — 'we turned that kid into an animal' — based on a training regimen of: being hit with trash cans, punching boards badly, and getting drunk
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony of Dennis's confidence is well-earned by this point. The audience knows exactly what 'training' involved; Dennis is genuinely proud. Good setup for the inevitable collapse.

jokes.text: Dee's roid-rage interior monologue: 'CALL ME A HOLOCAUST VICTIM? SAY YOU'RE PRETTIER THAN ME?' / 'OKAY, MAYBE THAT PART MIGHT BE A LITTLE BIT TRUE.'
jokes.setup: Dee is psyching herself up pre-fight, running through Bobby's insults to fuel her rage
jokes.punchline: Mid-rage-fueling monologue, Dee momentarily concedes that Bobby might be prettier than her — a flash of honest self-assessment in the middle of steroid mania
jokes.explanation: Brilliant comedic beat. Dee is building herself up for a fight by replaying insults... then pauses to genuinely consider whether Bobby is prettier than her and concludes 'maybe that part might be a little bit true.' The honesty puncturing the rage is unexpected and character-perfect. The rhythm — confident rage, then hesitation, then honest concession — is impeccably structured.

jokes.text: Dee discovers someone took her steroids: 'WHO TOOK MY SHIT?' / Frank: 'I MIGHT HAVE HAD SOME.'
jokes.setup: Dee is looking for her steroid supply before the fight
jokes.punchline: Frank casually admits to having taken some of Dee's steroids — his understatement 'I might have had some' implies he's also been dosing himself
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Frank has been secretly taking Dee's steroids is unexpected and darkly funny. 'I might have had some' is perfect Frank delivery — casual, slightly sheepish, as if he borrowed a casserole dish. The implication that Frank is also on steroids sets up his later fight with Bobby.

jokes.text: Frank on steroids confronts Dee: 'WHAT DID YOU JUST SAY, YOU LITTLE BITCH?' — 69-year-old Frank full roid-rage
jokes.setup: Frank has taken Dee's steroids; Dee is furious
jokes.punchline: Frank — an elderly, grotesque man — is now ALSO fully roid-raged, calling Dee a 'little bitch' and threatening to 'punch a hole through your face'
jokes.explanation: The steroid subplot reaches its peak with Frank — the most inappropriate candidate for roid rage — squaring off with Dee. Frank's physical threat to a person who is already in a rage is perfectly escalated. Two roid-ragers fighting each other is the logical and absurd conclusion of this thread.

jokes.text: Dee threatens: 'I am gonna rip your face off... make a shirt out of it, and I'm gonna wear it.'
jokes.setup: Dee has discovered Charlie took her steroids and is now threatening him
jokes.punchline: The threat escalates from violence to craft project — Dee will fashion Charlie's face into a wearable garment
jokes.explanation: Exceptional escalation. The threat doesn't stop at face-ripping — Dee has planned the full post-violence workflow: face removal, shirt manufacture, wearing it. The specificity and the domestic craft-project framing of extreme violence is very funny. 'I'm gonna wear it' as the final step is the perfect button. Near the episode's best material.

jokes.text: Dee, in full roid rage, announces: 'I'M GONNA TAKE ONE SECOND TO TAKE MY SHIRT OFF, AND THEN YOU'RE GONNA DIE!'
jokes.setup: Dee and Frank are threatening each other in a full mutual roid-rage confrontation; Dee is promising death
jokes.punchline: In the middle of an unhinged death threat, Dee adds the shirt-removal step as a procedural necessity — connecting back to Charlie's shirt refusal from earlier, but now it's Dee, pre-murder, calmly noting she needs to remove her shirt first
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a masterful callback. The shirt-removal running gag — which ran through the Charlie training subplot — is paid off here in the most unexpected context. Dee, in full homicidal roid rage, pauses her death threat to note she needs to remove her shirt first. The structure is perfect: 'I'm gonna take one second to take my shirt off' (procedural, matter-of-fact) 'and then you're gonna die' (the death threat). The callback works because it recontextualizes the entire shirt gag as an episode-wide theme. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: A passing stranger tells Frank and Dee to take their fight elsewhere: 'YOU WANNA BEAT UP ON YOUR LITTLE BOYFRIEND, YOU GO DO IT SOMEWHERE ELSE.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dee are screaming at each other in what appears to be outside a bar
jokes.punchline: A stranger observing the scene misreads Frank (elderly, grotesque) as Dee's 'little boyfriend' — an insult to both and a funny misread of their family relationship
jokes.explanation: The 'little boyfriend' label for Frank is funny but it's an easy joke. Competent but not among the episode's stronger moments. Functions to move the scene along.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Where the hell is your fighter?' Dennis: 'He'll be here.' Mac: 'He'll be here WHEN?' Dennis: 'SOON!'
jokes.setup: The fight is about to start and Charlie hasn't arrived
jokes.punchline: Dennis's increasingly desperate non-answers — 'he'll be here,' 'soon!' — without any actual information, delivered with diminishing confidence
jokes.explanation: Functional tension-building comedy. The escalating desperation in 'SOON!' is a minor beat. Not particularly crafted but serves its purpose.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis discover Charlie is in jail — 'APPARENTLY THEY GOT ALL HOPPED UP ON AMPHETAMINES AND BEAT THE SHIT OUT OF SOME GUY IN FRONT OF THE BAR.' / 'AMPHETAMINES? YEAH, LIKE, STEROIDS OR SOMETHING. I DON'T KNOW.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are at the underground fight waiting for Charlie; he never shows
jokes.punchline: The payoff to the steroid subplot: Charlie (and presumably Dee) got arrested for assault while hopped up on what Mac vaguely describes as 'amphetamines? Like steroids or something'
jokes.explanation: The steroid payoff landing off-screen is a good structural choice — we get the result without the scene. Mac's chemical vagueness ('amphetamines? Like, steroids or something. I don't know.') is characteristically ignorant. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The reveal: Charlie and Dee are both in jail, having 'gotten all hopped up on amphetamines and beat the shit out of some guy in front of the bar.'
jokes.setup: Mac gets off the phone with Charlie, explaining his absence
jokes.punchline: The completely logical but maximally disastrous outcome — both fighters are in jail for drug-fueled assault
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the steroid plotlines — both fighters simultaneously arrested before their respective matches — is a satisfying structural joke. 'All hopped up on amphetamines' is a good phrasing.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis look at the scrawny opponent Charlie was supposed to fight: 'LOOK AT THE DUDE HE WAS SUPPOSED TO FIGHT. HE'S THE SCRAWNIEST...' / 'CHARLIE WOULD HAVE KILLED THAT GUY.' / 'ANYBODY COULD KICK THAT GUY'S ASS.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis lament Charlie missing the fight
jokes.punchline: The opponent is comically scrawny — their lament about missing the money transitions to Dennis suggesting Mac could fight him instead
jokes.explanation: The punchline is implicit: the scrawny opponent means anyone could win, which means their fight money is recoverable. Dennis's pivot to suggesting Mac fight — with 'you're, like, the second toughest guy I know' — is good Mac characterization (he'll believe anything flattering).

jokes.text: 'OH, MY GOD. YEAH. YEAH. OH, YOU'RE, LIKE, THE SECOND TOUGHEST GUY I KNOW.' / 'I DID BASH CHARLIE GOOD A COUPLE TIMES.' / 'YOU ALMOST HURT HIM ONCE. WITH THE BOTTLE?' / 'YEAH, AND THAT'S NEXT TO IMPOSSIBLE. THAT WAS GOOD.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is convincing Mac to fight in Charlie's place
jokes.punchline: Dennis's flattery ('second toughest guy I know') is immediately revealed to be manipulative; Mac's credential is that he 'almost hurt' Charlie once with a bottle — presented as a remarkable achievement
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to Charlie's 'practically invincible' status from earlier. The fact that Mac's greatest fighting credential is 'almost hurting' Charlie once — and Dennis validates this as 'next to impossible, that was good' — perfectly encapsulates the gang's warped hierarchy. Dennis's manipulation of Mac via minimal flattery is a core character dynamic beautifully compressed.

jokes.text: Dennis tells the bookie 'Clown Baby has arrived' — meaning Mac is now Clown Baby
jokes.setup: Dennis has just convinced Mac to fight; he goes to inform the bookie
jokes.punchline: The 'Clown Baby' name, established earlier as a strategic underdog brand, now refers to Mac — who doesn't know Dennis has switched the bet
jokes.explanation: The 'Clown Baby has arrived' line lands with the comedic weight of everything that's been built. The audience knows something Mac doesn't — Dennis is about to bet against him. Rewatch bonus for the layered dramatic irony.

jokes.text: Bobby says Dee 'chickened out' — Frank offers himself as the replacement fighter: 'YOU WANT YOUR FIGHT? YOU GOT YOUR FIGHT. YOU AND ME, RIGHT NOW.'
jokes.setup: Bobby gloats that Dee didn't show up for their arranged fight
jokes.punchline: Frank — an old, out-of-shape man who has been taking steroids and can barely function — challenges Bobby, who is similarly aged and decrepit, to a fight 'right now'
jokes.explanation: The parallel resolution — Frank steps in as his own daughter's replacement — mirrors Mac stepping in for Charlie. Two old men on steroids fighting is the right absurd payoff for the Frank/Bobby subplot. Frank's declaration is delivered with appropriate insane bravado.

jokes.text: Bobby, hearing Dee is arrested: 'Ah! I knew that skinny bitch would chicken out.' Frank: 'So we'll never get the fight.' Bobby: 'That's a shame, Frankie. Lot of unanswered questions.'
jokes.setup: Frank reveals Dee has been arrested and can't fight
jokes.punchline: 'Lot of unanswered questions' — Bobby reframing a missed fight as a philosophical gap rather than just a scheduling conflict
jokes.explanation: 'Lot of unanswered questions' applied to a boxing match is a good bit of pomposity from Bobby. Decent character moment.

jokes.text: Mac says 'I gave it my best.' Dennis: 'YEAH. YOU KNOW WHAT? YOUR BEST WASN'T GOOD ENOUGH.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to process his humiliating defeat
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers the inspirational sports-movie phrase 'your best wasn't good enough' — which is technically true but completely anti-inspirational — with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion of the sports-movie catchphrase. 'Your best wasn't good enough' exists in motivational culture as a push to do better — delivered here as a cold, accurate fact. Dennis's sincerity makes it devastating and funny simultaneously. Excellent economy — six words, full impact. Quotable.

jokes.text: The same mugger reappears to rob Mac and Dennis after the fight: 'HEY, YOU HAVE THE TIME?' / 'AW, NOT YOU AGAIN.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis have just lost all their money in the fight; they're in an alley
jokes.punchline: The opening episode mugger returns — using the same 'have the time?' approach — and Mac's weary 'not you again' implies this is an ongoing pattern
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural callback — the episode bookends with the same mugger. 'Not you again' implies a regularity to the mugging relationship that is both absurd and character-illuminating (of course these guys get regularly mugged by the same person). The circular structure is well-engineered.

jokes.text: The same mugger reappears: 'Hey, you have the time?' Mac: 'Aw, not you again.' — the original mugger from the opening has found them again
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are broke and defeated after the fight
jokes.punchline: The same mugger from the opening returns — the gang has come full circle and is now being robbed again, with less money than before
jokes.explanation: The structural callback — same mugger, same alley, now Mac and Dennis are the vulnerable ones Dee warned about — is satisfying episode architecture. 'Aw, not you again' implies they recognize him, which raises the question of how often this gang gets mugged by the same guy.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis try to explain they have no money; mugger threatens to stab them; Dennis refuses to empty his pockets 'on principle': 'IT'S A MATTER OF PRINCIPLE. I DON'T FEEL LIKE STANDING IN AN ALLEY WITH A METH-HEAD.'
jokes.setup: The mugger is threatening to stab them if they don't empty their pockets; Mac complies
jokes.punchline: Dennis refuses — not from bravery but from an aesthetic objection to the situation. His 'principle' is that he simply doesn't feel like standing in an alley with a meth-head, as if this is a reasonable position to take against a stabbing threat
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Dennis. His objection to the mugging isn't fear-based or brave — it's rooted in personal inconvenience and aesthetic preference. 'I don't feel like standing in an alley with a meth-head' as a 'principle' is a magnificent window into Dennis's sociopathic self-regard. High character integration: this could only be Dennis.

jokes.text: Dennis refuses to empty his pockets on 'a matter of principle': 'I don't feel like standing in an alley with a meth-head.'
jokes.setup: Mugger demands Dennis empty his pockets; Dennis refuses
jokes.punchline: Dennis's principled refusal to comply with an armed mugger as a matter of dignity — 'it's a matter of principle' said while being threatened with stabbing
jokes.explanation: Very Dennis — his ego and sense of dignity override basic survival instinct. 'I don't feel like standing in an alley with a meth-head' as a reason not to comply with an armed robbery is perfect narcissist logic.

jokes.text: Dennis produces a large wad of cash from his pocket — he had bet against Mac
jokes.setup: Dennis has been refusing to show his pockets; under pressure he finally does, revealing the cash
jokes.punchline: The cash reveals Dennis secretly bet against Mac winning the fight — he profited from Mac's beatdown
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands hard — Dennis has been playing both sides the entire time, manipulating Mac into fighting while betting on Mac's loss. It recontextualizes the 'Clown Baby has arrived' scene. High character integration: this is exactly what Dennis would do. The mugger as the agent of reveal is structurally elegant.

jokes.text: Mac: 'WHY WOULD YOU BET AGAINST ME?' / Dennis: 'IT WAS THE RIGHT MOVE.' / Mac: 'I COULD HAVE TAKEN A DIVE. I WOULDN'T HAVE HAD TO GET MY ASS KICKED.' / Dennis: 'MAC, IT HAD TO LOOK REAL.'
jokes.setup: Mac discovers Dennis bet against him
jokes.punchline: Mac's legitimate grievance — he could have thrown the fight without the actual beating — exposes that Dennis's 'it had to look real' is cover for the fact that he didn't tell Mac the plan. Dennis's calm justification makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: The 'it had to look real' justification is Dennis at his most coldly manipulative. Mac's point is entirely reasonable (he could have faked it) and Dennis's counter is exposed as self-serving. The exchange is a perfect window into their friendship's power dynamic.

jokes.text: Mac: 'WERE YOU GONNA TELL ME EVENTUALLY?' / [pause] Dennis: 'YES.' / [pause] 'YEAH?'
jokes.setup: Mac is demanding to know if Dennis would have eventually confessed to the scheme
jokes.punchline: Dennis's 'Yes' followed by a beat — the pause making clear it's a lie — then Mac's skeptical 'Yeah?' daring him to maintain it. Dennis says 'I was going to tell you eventually' with no conviction.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the pauses. Dennis's 'Yes' is delivered into silence; Mac's skeptical 'Yeah?' is a beat later. Then Dennis repeats a longer, fully unconvincing version of the same claim. The transcript captures the rhythm with the line breaks. High economy — the words are almost irrelevant, the timing is everything. Exceptional character integration: Dennis cannot genuinely commit to a simple admission.

jokes.text: Mac tells the mugger to stab Dennis: 'YOU KNOW WHAT? STAB THIS SON OF A BITCH.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been betrayed by Dennis and is furious
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to being betrayed by his friend is to instruct the mugger currently threatening them to redirect the stabbing toward Dennis
jokes.explanation: Perfect dark escalation. Mac weaponizes the mugging against Dennis — the threat that was terrorizing them becomes a tool of interpersonal conflict. 'Stab this son of a bitch' is the most direct possible expression of Mac's fury. Very quotable in context.

jokes.text: Mac's response to Dennis's betrayal: 'You know what? Stab this son of a bitch.' — ordering the mugger to stab Dennis
jokes.setup: Mac has finally processed Dennis's betrayal and decides on a response
jokes.punchline: Mac's resolution is to deputize the mugger — their active assailant — to punish Dennis on his behalf
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a quintessential IASIP moment. Mac is so furious at Dennis that he repurposes the mugger as an instrument of justice — turning a robbery into a targeted assassination order. 'Stab this son of a bitch' is the most efficient possible expression of Mac's betrayal feelings, and the fact that it's addressed to an armed mugger who he's cooperating with is insane. Perfect character logic, tremendous economy, completely unexpected. Very close to the 8.5 anchor quality.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'PLEASE DON'T STAB ME.' — to the mugger, sincerely
jokes.setup: Mac has instructed the mugger to stab Dennis; Dennis is now genuinely in danger from his own friend's directive
jokes.punchline: Dennis's dignified, plaintive 'please don't stab me' — said to a meth-head mugger — is funny in its politeness and in the fact that Mac has actually created a credible stabbing threat toward him
jokes.explanation: The polite register of 'please don't stab me' in this context is the joke — Dennis maintaining a certain dignity even when asking a meth-head to spare his life. Brief, economical, perfectly placed.

jokes.text: Bobby and Frank's old-man grudge match setup: 'Seeing that we're a couple of old men here, I think we should lay down some ground rules. Now. Number one.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Bobby are about to finally settle their decades-old grudge
jokes.punchline: The elaborate 'ground rules' setup — implying a nuanced negotiation between two honorable old fighters — which then presumably gives way to immediate chaos (cut to 'Holy shit!')
jokes.explanation: The setup is in the deliberate, stately 'ground rules' speech — implying dignity — followed immediately by the cut to 'Holy shit!' which suggests the fight immediately descended into chaos without any ground rules being established. The structure uses the gap between scenes as the punchline. Good misdirection.

jokes.text: 'HOLY SHIT!' — the episode's final line, following the implied Frank/Bobby fight
jokes.setup: Frank has just begun establishing ground rules for his fight with Bobby
jokes.punchline: The episode ends on 'HOLY SHIT!' — implying the fight either began immediately without rules or the rules themselves were shocking
jokes.explanation: The final button of the episode. Two words ending a 22-minute escalation. What happened? We don't know. That's the joke. The unseen is funnier than anything that could have been depicted. Perfect final punctuation.

tmdb_overview: Frank runs into an old adversary at the gym when he begins teaching Dee to box after she was robbed. Hoping to make some extra money on the side, Mac and Dennis make preparations for Charlie to compete in an underground street fighting match.
